_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss (Tomás trusted by his boss vs Ravi treated as an adult by customers; Grace's racing heart vs Ellen's lasting habit). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 3.
title: My first job
subtitle: Four people look back on the job they did as teenagers.

sections.A: Tomás, 41, architect. The summer I turned sixteen, a friend of my father's who owned two ice-cream vans on the coast needed someone for weekends, and I was told, rather than asked, that I'd be doing it. I was horrified. The uniform was a pink and white striped shirt, and the beach was exactly where everyone from my school spent their Saturdays. For the first fortnight I hid in the back of the van whenever I recognised anyone. What changed things was that after only a week the owner left me in charge of a van on my own, with the cash box and the keys. Nobody had ever trusted me with anything like that before, and I wasn't going to let him down. I stopped caring about the shirt. I've managed much bigger budgets since, but I've never felt quite so responsible for anything.
sections.B: Grace, 35, doctor. My first job was washing dishes in a hotel kitchen, three evenings a week, when I was fifteen. The head chef shouted constantly, not at anyone in particular, just at the general situation, and on my first night I assumed I'd be sacked before midnight. I wasn't, and gradually I understood that the shouting wasn't personal; it was simply how the kitchen kept moving when everything was going wrong at once. I work in an emergency department now, and I sometimes think that kitchen prepared me better than medical school did for a busy Saturday night. The pay was terrible. I spent my first week's wages on a scarf for my mother, who wore it every winter until it fell apart. I still can't walk past a hotel kitchen door without my heart beating a little faster.
sections.C: Ravi, 29, software developer. My father ran a corner shop, and from the age of thirteen I worked there after school. For the first two years he didn't pay me at all; he said I was 'learning the business', which at the time sounded like an excuse. I resented it enormously, especially when my friends were out playing football. It was years before I understood what he'd been doing: teaching me how to talk to strangers, how to stay polite when someone was rude, how to notice when an elderly customer hadn't been in for a few days. The customers were the best part. They told me about their lives as if I were an adult, and I think that's when I started to behave like one.
sections.D: Ellen, 52, journalist. At seventeen I got a job as an usher in the town's only cinema. The films changed every fortnight, so I'd often see the same one forty times, and I became an expert on audiences rather than films: who laughed first, who cried, who was secretly checking their watch. I started writing notes about them in a little book. Unfortunately I also chatted to the other ushers during the quieter scenes, and after a warning that I chose to ignore, I was dismissed. I was furious at the time, but I'd kept the notebook. A year later I used those notes in my first article for the local paper, a piece about what people reveal about themselves in the dark. I've been a journalist ever since, and I still watch the audience more than the screen.

questions.question: Which person had their first job chosen for them by someone else?
questions.why: 'I was told, rather than asked, that I'd be doing it.' Ravi worked for his father, but nothing says he was made to start.

questions.question: Which person came to see that a boss's apparently angry behaviour had a practical purpose?
questions.why: The shouting 'wasn't personal; it was simply how the kitchen kept moving'.

questions.question: Which person lost the job because of their own behaviour?
questions.why: She chatted during films and ignored a warning, so 'I was dismissed'.

questions.question: Which person was embarrassed at first to be seen at work by people they knew?
questions.why: The striped shirt on the beach where his school spent Saturdays: 'I hid in the back of the van whenever I recognised anyone'.

questions.question: Which person believes the job prepared them for their present work better than formal training did?
questions.why: 'That kitchen prepared me better than medical school did for a busy Saturday night.'

questions.question: Which person received no money for their work at first?
questions.why: 'For the first two years he didn't pay me at all.' Grace was paid, if badly.

questions.question: Which person still has a physical reaction to a certain kind of place?
questions.why: 'I still can't walk past a hotel kitchen door without my heart beating a little faster.' Ellen's lasting habit is a way of watching, not a physical reaction.

questions.question: Which person has kept a habit that began during the job?
questions.why: 'I still watch the audience more than the screen.'

questions.question: Which person started to act in a more grown-up way because of how the public treated them?
questions.why: Customers 'told me about their lives as if I were an adult, and I think that's when I started to behave like one'. Tomás was trusted by the owner, not by the public.

questions.question: Which person used something from the job to start their career?
questions.why: Her cinema notebook became 'my first article for the local paper'.
